questions.q: In a checkout, which step should stay in the request instead of moving to a background job?
questions.explain: The answer to the customer depends on the payment and the saved order. Everything that only needs to happen eventually (receipts, invoices, analytics) can be queued, so it is retried on failure instead of failing the checkout.
options: E-mailing the receipt
Rendering the PDF invoice
Charging the card and saving the order
Telling the analytics service about the sale

questions.q: What is the difference between a job and an event?
questions.explain: "Send the receipt for order 1001" is a job. "Order 1001 was paid" is an event: e-mail, warehouse and loyalty can each react, and a new feature can subscribe without changing the producer.
options: Jobs are JSON, events are binary
A job is an instruction for one handler; an event is a fact that any number of subscribers may react to
Events are always processed before jobs
Jobs can be retried, events cannot

questions.q: Why does a worker claim a job (hide it for a while) instead of removing it from the queue?
questions.explain: Only an ack deletes a job. A lease (visibility timeout) makes a crashed worker's job reappear, which is what turns crashes into retries.
options: Removing jobs is slow
If the worker dies before acking, the lease runs out and the job becomes available again instead of being lost
So two workers can process it at the same time
Because the queue has to count attempts

questions.q: What does at-least-once delivery promise?
questions.explain: Redelivery after a crash is how nothing gets lost, and it is also why duplicates happen. The consumer must be idempotent to turn that into an exactly-once effect.
options: Every message is processed exactly once
No message is lost, but a message may be delivered more than once
Messages arrive in the order they were sent
A message is delivered at most once, and may be lost

questions.q: A vendor promises "exactly-once delivery". What should you still do?
questions.explain: Across a network, a consumer can always do the work and crash before its acknowledgement arrives. Exactly-once is achieved inside a system, or as exactly-once effect through idempotency, never as a promise you can skip.
options: Nothing; duplicates are impossible now
Make consumers with important effects idempotent anyway
Turn off retries
Process messages in a single thread

questions.q: PDF jobs take about 40 seconds, and the visibility timeout is 30 seconds. What happens?
questions.explain: The queue cannot tell a slow worker from a dead one. The lease must be longer than a normal run, or long jobs must extend it with a heartbeat.
options: The jobs fail with a timeout error
Each job is handed to a second worker while the first is still working, so PDFs are rendered twice
Nothing, the timeout only matters after a crash
The queue waits until the first worker finishes

questions.q: Why do retries wait longer after each failure (exponential backoff)?
questions.explain: Short outages are handled by the first quick retries; longer ones by the later, spaced-out ones, without hammering the service the moment it comes back.
options: To use fewer attempts in total
A service that is down needs time to recover, and retrying fast only adds load and wastes attempts
Because queues can only schedule in powers of two
To keep jobs in order

questions.q: 1,000 receipt jobs failed at 12:00:00 because the mail provider was down. What does jitter add to their retries?
questions.explain: Without jitter, every job retries at 12:00:01, 12:00:03, and so on together: a new spike each time. Randomness turns the spikes into a steady stream.
options: It makes them retry immediately
It spreads their retry times, so they do not all hit the provider in the same second
It stops them after a random number of attempts
It changes their order

questions.q: A receipt job has the address bola.example.com. What should happen?
questions.explain: No retry can fix bad data. Retrying wastes work and delays the problem; deleting hides it. The dead-letter queue keeps it where people will see and fix it.
options: Retry it with backoff until it works
Retry it forever at a slow rate
Treat it as a permanent failure and move it to the dead-letter queue at once
Delete it silently

questions.q: Which API answer should normally be treated as transient (worth retrying)?
questions.explain: 5xx answers, timeouts and 429 (too many requests) usually pass. Most 4xx answers mean the request itself is wrong, so the same request will fail again.
options: 400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
503 Service Unavailable
422 Unprocessable Content

questions.q: What should a team do with the dead-letter queue?
questions.explain: Dead letters are work that did not get done: receipts not sent, points not credited. They are an inbox for engineers, not a bin.
options: Empty it every night
Alert when it is not empty, fix the cause, then replay the dead jobs
Ignore it; those jobs were bad anyway
Retry its jobs automatically every minute

questions.q: What is a poison message?
questions.explain: It might be malformed data or a bug that one specific payload triggers. maxAttempts and the dead-letter queue stop it from looping.
options: A message sent by an attacker
A message that fails every time it is processed, and would block or waste workers if retried forever
A message larger than the queue allows
A message without an id

questions.q: Which consumer is naturally idempotent?
questions.explain: Setting a value to the same thing twice leaves the same result. Adding, sending and transferring change something each time, so they need deduplication.
options: "Add 204 loyalty points to customer 8"
"Set order 1001's status to shipped"
"Send an SMS to +2348031234567"
"Transfer ₦5,000 to the seller"

questions.q: Why must the "processed message" record be written in the same transaction as the loyalty-points update?
questions.explain: Both writes commit together or not at all. Any split between them opens a window where a crash causes a duplicate or a loss.
options: Because PostgreSQL requires it
So a crash cannot leave points credited but the message unrecorded (double credit next time), or recorded but not credited (lost credit)
To make the query faster
So the message can be read by other consumers

questions.q: In the lesson's consumer, what does INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING message_id tell the code?
questions.explain: The primary key lets exactly one insert succeed. The others hit the conflict, return no row, and the consumer skips the effect.
options: How many times the message was delivered
Whether this delivery is the first one: a returned row means "first", no row means "already processed"
Whether the database is available
The customer's new balance

questions.q: The effect is an e-mail through an outside provider, so it cannot share your database transaction. What is the best available protection against duplicates?
questions.explain: With an idempotency key, the provider itself ignores a repeated request. Without one, a rare duplicate remains possible, which for e-mail is usually acceptable.
options: Sending the e-mail twice to be safe
Passing the message id to the provider as an idempotency key, if it supports one
Deleting the job before sending
Using a longer visibility timeout

questions.q: The checkout saves the order and then adds a job to Redis. Redis is unreachable for that one call. What is the result?
questions.explain: Two systems cannot be updated in one transaction. This "dual write" problem is what the transactional outbox solves.
options: The database rolls back the order automatically
The order exists but its job does not; nothing will ever send the receipt
Redis stores the job when it comes back
The job is added twice

questions.q: How does the transactional outbox avoid losing messages?
questions.explain: The order and its message commit together in the one system that has transactions. Publishing becomes a separate, retryable step.
options: It retries the enqueue in the request until it succeeds
The message is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order; a relay publishes it later and retries until it succeeds
It writes the order to the queue instead of the database
It uses exactly-once delivery

questions.q: What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do in the relay's query?
questions.explain: Several relays (or workers) can then share one table safely. The same query is the heart of a PostgreSQL-backed job queue.
options: Deletes the selected rows
Locks the rows this relay takes, and makes other relays skip them instead of waiting or sending them twice
Reads rows without any lock
Skips rows that were already sent

questions.q: The relay publishes three outbox rows and crashes before its transaction commits. What happens next?
questions.explain: The relay is at-least-once too. That is why it derives the job id from the outbox row id, and why consumers are idempotent regardless.
options: The three messages are lost
The rows are still unsent, so the next run publishes them again; job ids and idempotent consumers absorb the repeat
The database marks them as sent anyway
The queue rejects all future messages
The rows are moved to the dead-letter queue

questions.q: Why does each subscriber of order.paid get its own queue?
questions.explain: Separate queues mean separate retries, backlogs and dead letters. E-mail keeps flowing while the warehouse catches up.
options: To save memory
So a slow or failing subscriber (say, the warehouse) cannot delay or block the others
Because a queue can only hold one job type
To guarantee global ordering

questions.q: With retries and several workers, can a consumer rely on jobs finishing in the order they were enqueued?
questions.explain: A job that is retried after 8 seconds finishes after jobs added later. Where order matters, carry a version and ignore older updates, or use a broker that orders per key.
options: Yes, queues are always first-in first-out
No: retries and parallel workers reorder jobs; design consumers so order does not matter, or use versions
Yes, if the visibility timeout is long enough
Only for dead letters

questions.q: What should a "send receipt" message contain?
questions.explain: Small payloads avoid stale copies and keep sensitive data out of queues, which are logged and inspected. Validate the payload in the consumer: it is outside data.
options: The whole order, the customer's card number and their password hash, so the consumer has everything
The order id (and little else); the consumer loads the current data itself
The rendered HTML of the e-mail
Nothing; the consumer guesses the order

questions.q: Which metric best shows customers are waiting too long for background work?
questions.explain: A queue can hold many jobs and still be fine if they are fresh. The oldest job's age is the delay a customer actually feels. Watch it together with the failure rate and the dead-letter count.
options: The number of workers
The age of the oldest waiting job
The size of each payload
The number of job types

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The delay doubles from 1 second and is capped at 30 seconds, so the sixth and seventh attempts wait 30 seconds instead of 32 and 64.

questions.q: A job fails at t = 0 and on every retry. With these delays, when does each attempt run?
questions.explain: After attempt 1 the job waits 1 s, after attempt 2 it waits 2 s, after attempt 3 it waits 4 s. So the attempts run at 0, 1, 3 and 7 seconds, as in the lesson's outage replay.
options: attempt 1 at 0s, attempt 2 at 1s, attempt 3 at 2s, attempt 4 at 3s then dead
attempt 1 at 0s, attempt 2 at 1s, attempt 3 at 3s, attempt 4 at 7s then dead
attempt 1 at 0s, attempt 2 at 2s, attempt 3 at 4s, attempt 4 at 8s then dead
attempt 1 at 1s, attempt 2 at 3s, attempt 3 at 7s, attempt 4 at 15s then dead

questions.q: A worker claims a job with a 30-second lease and never acks. What does this print?
questions.explain: The job is invisible for exactly 30 seconds. At 30 s the lease has run out and it is claimed again (attempt 2), which starts a new lease, so at 45 s it is hidden again.
options:
[
  '0s: claimed, attempt 1',
  '10s: claimed, attempt 2',
  '29.999s: claimed, attempt 3',
  '30s: claimed, attempt 4',
  '45s: claimed, attempt 5'
]

[
  '0s: claimed, attempt 1',
  '10s: hidden',
  '29.999s: hidden',
  '30s: claimed, attempt 2',
  '45s: hidden'
]

[
  '0s: claimed, attempt 1',
  '10s: hidden',
  '29.999s: hidden',
  '30s: hidden',
  '45s: claimed, attempt 2'
]
[ '0s: claimed, attempt 1', '10s: hidden', '29.999s: hidden', '30s: hidden', '45s: hidden' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An id derived from the business event (order-1001-receipt) makes a repeated enqueue harmless. The job with a generic id does not know it describes the same work, so it is a real duplicate.
options: 4 [ 'order-1001-receipt', 'order-1001-receipt', 'order-1002-receipt', 'job-1' ]
3 [ 'order-1001-receipt', 'order-1002-receipt', 'job-1' ]
2 [ 'order-1001-receipt', 'order-1002-receipt' ]
3 [ 'order-1001-receipt', 'order-1002-receipt', 'job-1.5' ]

questions.q: The same message is delivered three times. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every redelivery adds points in the naive consumer. The idempotent one remembers the message id and skips repeats. In production the processed ids live in the database, in the same transaction as the points.
options: { naive: 204, idempotent: 204 }
{ naive: 612, idempotent: 204 }
{ naive: 612, idempotent: 612 }
{ naive: 204, idempotent: 0 }

questions.q: Three jobs are enqueued in order; the second fails once and is retried after 2 seconds. In what order do they finish?
questions.explain: The retried job finishes last, although it was enqueued second. If these were price updates applied blindly, the final price would be price 2's, which is not the newest. Carry a version, or design updates so order does not matter.
options: [ 'update-price-1', 'update-price-2', 'update-price-3' ]
[ 'update-price-1', 'update-price-3', 'update-price-2' ]
[ 'update-price-2', 'update-price-1', 'update-price-3' ]
[ 'update-price-1', 'update-price-3' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Server errors, timeouts (408) and "too many requests" (429) may pass later. Bad requests, missing resources and invalid content will fail the same way every time.
options: 503:retry 400:retry 429:retry 404:retry 500:retry 422:retry
503:retry 400:dead 429:retry 404:dead 500:retry 422:dead
503:retry 400:dead 429:dead 404:dead 500:retry 422:dead
503:dead 400:dead 429:retry 404:dead 500:dead 422:dead

questions.q: An event is published twice (the producer retried). Each subscriber derives its job id from the event id. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each queue gets one copy per distinct event. The repeated order-1001-paid maps to the same job ids, so it adds nothing.
options: email=3 warehouse=3 loyalty=3
email=2 warehouse=2 loyalty=2
email=1 warehouse=1 loyalty=1
email=6 warehouse=0 loyalty=0

questions.q: The relay fails to publish and its transaction rolls back. What does this print?
questions.explain: The UPDATE ran, but the error rolled the whole transaction back, so both rows are still unsent. The next run publishes them. Nothing is lost, and nothing is marked sent before it really was.
options:
queue unreachable - unsent: 0
published 0 - unsent: 0

queue unreachable - unsent: 2
published 2 - unsent: 0

queue unreachable - unsent: 2
published 0 - unsent: 2

published 2 - unsent: 0
published 0 - unsent: 0

questions.q: This queue deletes a job the moment a worker takes it. The worker crashes while sending. What does this print?
questions.explain: Deleting on take is at-most-once delivery: no duplicates, but the crashed worker's job is gone for good. Receipt 1001 is never sent, and nothing records that it was lost.
options: sent: [ 'receipt 1001', 'receipt 1002' ] left in queue: 0
sent: [ 'receipt 1002' ] left in queue: 0
sent: [ 'receipt 1002' ] left in queue: 1
sent: [] left in queue: 2

questions.q: A consumer keeps processed ids in memory. The worker restarts between deliveries. What does this print?
questions.explain: The repeat before the restart was skipped, but the restart wiped the memory, so the redelivery after it was credited again. Processed ids must be stored durably, in the database, with the effect.
options: credits: 1
credits: 2
credits: 3
credits: 0

questions.q: Write backoff(attempt): 500 ms for attempt 1, doubling each attempt, never more than 10,000 ms.
questions.explain: 2 ** (attempt - 1) doubles the delay each time, and Math.min applies the cap so late attempts do not wait minutes.

questions.q: Write withEqualJitter(delayMs, random): half the delay is fixed, the other half is scaled by random() (a number from 0 to 1).
questions.explain: The delay stays between half and all of the exponential value: long enough to give the service room, random enough to spread the herd. Passing random in makes it testable.

questions.q: Write fail(job, error, permanent): record the error; if the failure is permanent or job.attempts has reached MAX_ATTEMPTS, push the job to dead and return "dead"; otherwise set runAt to now + 1000 * 2^(attempts-1) and return "retry".
questions.explain: A transient failure with attempts left is rescheduled with backoff. A job out of attempts, or one that can never succeed, goes to the dead letters for a human to look at.

questions.q: Write claim(now): return the first job whose runAt and leasedUntil are both <= now, after increasing its attempts and setting its lease to now + 30000; return undefined if none is ready.
questions.explain: At 1 s only job-2 is ready (job-1 waits for its retry at 5 s). Once claimed, job-2 is leased, so a second claim finds nothing. At 6 s job-1's retry time has come.

questions.q: Make creditPoints idempotent: remember processed message ids in processed, and skip a message whose id was already handled.
questions.explain: The second delivery of the same message is skipped; a different message is credited. With a database, the id goes into a table with a primary key, in the same transaction as the points.

questions.q: Write relay(publish) for an in-memory outbox: publish every row whose sentAt is null, with the job id outbox-ID, and mark only the rows that were published successfully.
questions.explain: Already-sent rows are skipped, and a row is marked only after its publish returned. If publish threw, the row would stay unsent and the next run would try again. The derived job id lets the queue ignore a repeat.

questions.q: Give enqueue a typed signature, so the payload must match the job type in ShopJobs. Then enqueue a receipt for order 1001 and print the queue.
questions.explain: K extends keyof ShopJobs ties the payload to the chosen type: a receipt without an e-mail, or a misspelt job type, no longer compiles. The consumer still validates the payload at runtime, because a stored message is outside data.
